projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Anthony Francis Galano was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Today is Saturday, April 28, 2007 and I am interviewing Mr. Anthony Francis Galano at his home in Silver Spring, Maryland. Mr. Galano was born on April 23, 1925 and is 82 years old. My name is Christopher Shaheen and I will be interviewing Mr. Galano who is my uncle's father-in-law and a surrogate grandfather to me. He is a graduate of Regis High School in New York City and an alumnus of Fordham University. Mr. Galano, would you please state for the record the war and branch of the service in which you served?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Yes, the war was World War II. The branch of service was the United States Navy.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Did you get drafted or did you enlist and what dates did you serve?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: No, I was not drafted. I enlisted on April 28, 1943, and I served on active duty until July 22, 1946.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What made you enlist?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: That's always a question that's asked me and I don't really know how you could prove that there is a cause-effect to it. But, it just seems like-I don't know if it's in you genes or your background or in you family's history. My father was an immigrant from Italy. He came over here when he was sixteen years old. He was born in 1897 and when he was over here, maybe the first year or so, the war broke out-World War I. And he enlisted in the United States Navy and served throughout the war on a transport-a troop transport called the U.S.S. Kroonland, taking soldiers back and forth across the Atlantic. But that was one possible reason that I sort of was fond of the Navy. Plus, another reason--every year, when I was younger, say six, five, six years old, we used to go away to the Jersey Shore for vacations. And I was always used to being in the water-and in the ocean. And, then, there's another strange possibility, that when I was ... How old was I - maybe, twelve or thirteen? I was a member of something called the Junior Naval Reserve. I have a photograph I have included in the Photograph Log. A picture someone took, I don't know who they were, probably a devoted family member. A picture of my platoon marching, this Junior Naval Reserve, we were only ten, twelve, thirteen years old, in the Memorial Day Parade on Riverside Drive in New York, Manhattan, New York. And, then, there is another interesting possibility that ... I'm trying to recall what year-it was a fleet appearance--they used to call it a fleet exercise that you came to New York City. I think I was probably about eight years old. It must have been about' 32, 1932 or 1933, where the North River, which is the Hudson River, in New York was just lined up with ships from this fleet, from our fleet, the United States Fleet. They had been out-being inspected by Roosevelt, Franklin Roosevelt, and they came into New York for liberty. And there I was, I probably was about seven or eight years old. I used to have a little notebook, a little small notebook, and I would be out on the street, down by the park, which was only about two blocks away from where I lived, meeting the sailors when they'd come off the ship, and asking them to sign my book and with their name and where their home town was. Now, this goes back quite a few years. So, all those things, I don't know that they were causative, but those are the only things I could put together that would make me want to be in the navy. Actually, I was selected for .. .I had passed all the exams for midshipmen school. The only difficulty was that, in order to get into middshipmen school or one of the requirements, was that you have two years of college. I had only had one year of college at that point because, as I say, when the war broke out, I was only sixteen years 0Id-1941. So, I took advantage of the Navy. They have--what they call a V-12 Program, where you ... They would send you to college. You had to enlist and go on active duty. But, they would send you to college for a year to make up whatever courses you were lacking that were required for that two year period-math courses, physics, that type. So that I attended the College of the Holy Cross for one year before being sent to midshipmen school. Is that a long answer? (chuckling)

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What was your family's response when they found out that you were enlisting?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I don't know. That's a good question, but I'm not sure, number one, that they had a response or that I can remember it. I'm sure they were ... you see, at the time, its hard to explain to people today, in the year 2007, what it was like in 1943 or "4", because the people were sort of traumatized by Pearl Harbor, with a pretty nasty, unprovoked attackkilling thousands of sailors and destroying most of our fleet. And the feeling, then, was that you had to enlist or become part of it, somehow or other, to ... as in your own defense. See that's why it's difficult for people to understand, like even my own children ... used to question me about the treatment that the Japanese nationalists received out ... mostly out in the west coast when they were interned. Now, it was a terrible thing to do, I understand that now. But when you put yourself back thirty or forty or fifty years into those days, when your ships ... your navy was destroyed, and you were expecting to get attacked and invaded, while it didn't make sense today, to do this to those people, it was a different time ... you can't .. .it's hard to explain.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What would be your response today if your son, Michael, told you that he enlisted in the Navy to serve in Iraq? What advice would you give him?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, it's a little difficult, for number one; he's too old for me to be giving him advice. But, let's say he was only seventeen or eighteen, I don't know ... I ... as I say, the times are very different today. And ... well, you see what's going on with the way ... the treatment that's involved, nowadays, with the troops and the people that are coming back. There is a different feeling in the country today. I sort of regret that the president has never put this country on a war footing, because And to, sort of. .. maybe have everyone serve a year maybe not in the armed serve but ... in some kind of a community or hospital ... just to get everybody back feeling they should do something for this country, because God-forbid we ever had to have ... a draft or standing army-I don't know where it would come from.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: How did you end up going to the Atlantic and Pacific Theaters?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, my usual answer to a question like that is .. , (chuckling), and I know it sounds trite, but it is not meant to be, is that I did .. .1 went where I was told to go and I did what I was told to do. So, as far as the Atlantic (coughs) - Excuse me was concerned, I had duty in various communication departments in the navy ... in different navy yards--Charleston navy yard was one ... South Carolina-- another. I was over in the Pacific-Pearl Harbor-in a communications location called Merco Pearl, which was a code-name for the work that we were doing in running convoys to the Pacific in World War II, which was a pretty scary time with the submarine threats, but um ... that's how I got to the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Tell me what the Hawaiian Sea Frontier was in detail.

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: That's actually umm ... The navy is like any other business. They have branch offices around the ... a company would have offices in different cities. They would have them over seas. Maybe ... well, the navy has naval districts going up and down the coast. They also have what they call sea frontiers. Now, the commander with the Hawaiian sea frontier was not necessarily in Hawaii. This was just like a general geographic area and he was located wherever he flew his flag. So, I happen to be in ... under his control in Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What was it like to be there? For instance, did you feel safe? What were the living conditions like?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: We lived in what they called BOQ's--which are Bachelor's Officer's Quarters. They were plain, usually; I guess you call them bunk beds-two beds ... four officers to a room. The BOQ I lived in had three decks and the first two decks were for most of us. The third deck was reserved for officers awaiting court marshal (chuckling). I don't say that in a joking ... joking fashion. But, the problem there was that most of them were either communicators or supply corpse officers. And if you think about it, those are the two easiest ways to get into trouble, because ... especially your communicator. When you are a communicator, you are responsible for registered publications which are anything from code books to different code machines and when you ... when you're in a command .. .if you're in charge and those books are assigned to you ... when you're at a change ofcommand ... when you ... when you're relieved or when you're relieving somebody, you have to account for every ... everything has a number to it. .. and you have to account for every piece of registered publication in your control because if .. .if there's one piece missing, it's assumed to be compromised and it cannot be used anymore. For example, even ships of the navy, airplanes, submarines, they all have different ... different ratings. For example, an airplane or submarine would not carry the amount or the type of code ... code book that a battleship would for the simple reason that if a plane was down or a submarine was sunk, you had no way of knowing if that code was compromised by somebody going down after it. So, it was a pretty complicated procedure.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: How did you escape injury?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I was never actually aware that, and I probably should have been, (chuckles) that ... uhh ... because, even on an island location, there were spies-there were Japanese spies there--and as an interesting point, how you meet people. I met an Army 1st Lieutenant when I went out there, that I had sort of grown up with when I was younger in New York when I was a kid. He was a New York City policeman and when he went over seas, he became a CID-Criminal Investigations of the Army. And he ended up in Hawaii and that's where I met him and he ... he was pretty famous out there. He was written up in all the newspapers for his ability ... He had captured quite a few spies.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What kinds of injuries did you witness?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Actually, since we weren't actually in a combat zone, per se, the only Japanese I ever saw there, were Prisoners of War. There was never that sort of a threat. I mean, it might have been there but like any other eighteen ... nineteen-year-old, you know you're going to live forever and you never really worry about thing like that.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: How were wounds and psychological problems handled? Or did you experience any?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Any of the what?

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Any psychological or...Any problems like that?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I think so, especially in that Pacific area, because ... This is one thing I'm .,. I won't say I'm amused today, because there's nothing funny about it. But...I don't understand. I mean ... there were things that .. .like the Bataan Death March that the Japanese conducted during the war in the Philippines and other things that they did. There were Prisoners of War that ended up in Japan and China working in factories ... They were being used for dangerous experiments. And today when I see what's going on in ... Iraq and Iran ... and the amount of attention that's being paid to it, I consider pretty small potatoes compared to what was going on during the war I knew. I don't understand why people ... although people today in this country are pretty much upset about everything, I guess. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Did you have any friendslbuddies who were prisoners of war?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Just one ... from the neighborhood where I grew up. He was captured by the Germans. I was never really very close to him other than knowing he was in the same city area that I was in. I never really knew him that well. In fact, he was about two years older than I was.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What were their experiences like as P.O.W.s? Were there any experiences that you knew about that he had?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: The fellow that was the Prisoner of War?

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: No, as I say, we were never .. .it's hard to explain. Well, maybe .. .like when you grow up .. .it's strange. Like I never knew my brother's friends. My brother is almost two years older than I am. And I. .. and maybe it's that waytoday---I don't know, but ... to his friends, I was a kid. So, I was not really in their group. So, now this fellow was in a group a year ahead of me. And ... In other words, you tended to keep within your age group. It is probably that way today, but I don't know.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Were you close with any soldiers who died in combat?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: No, I can't say that I was. Luckily. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: How did you cope with death and dying on the battlefield so that you could stay focused and protect yourselfl

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, as I say, I was in the Navy and I was never really in a battlefield. Unless you would consider a ship that gets sunk as a battlefield. I was never involved in that either except, it's one ofthe saddest things if you've seen pictures of ships that are being torpedoed, and destroyed and slipped down under the water. It's a pretty sad sight.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Why do you think you survived when others did not?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I don't...I know that question is asked ... I've seen it asked in movies and on television, but I don't know that it ever occurred to me to ask that question. I don't know. I really have no ... no recollection of thinking that way. Of course, now, you're going back almost eighty years ... or seventy years ( chuckles) and who knows what I was thinking about seventy years ago.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: In what ways did having a Jesuit education assist you? Did you resort to prayer?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I suspect ... uhh ... that one thing it did was that ... having the education I received .. .It taught me many things ... uhh ... mainly how to think, how to think clearly, how to ration-rationalize, problem solving. It was a good experience. And it was helpful, for sure.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What kind of support did you receive from family and friends while you were enlisted? For instance, did you receive letters and packages from home?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Mostly family, because when you ... when you're sixteen years old or seventeen at the time I guess, it wasn't a question of your friends sending you things. It was mostly your family that kept in touch---your cousins, your aunts or uncles. Letters were always welcomed. Packages ... It's a long way to send something and most of the time you can buy what you need.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Your highest rank was as a Commander. How did you earn that rank and what were your responsibilities/duties?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I was not actually a Commander in Hawaii; I became a Commander by staying active in the ready reserve after the war. When I say I became active in the ready reserve, what that meant was you were ... you were required to complete a certain amount of correspondence courses, naval war college courses. You would go on active duty two weeks every year. In addition to that, if you were a ... ifyou drilled with what they called a surface division, you would meet weekly. You would get fifty-two drills a year. You would meet for two or three hours once a week in uniform at an armory or some location with a reserve squadron. If you were a ... umm ... weekend warrior with the aft ... ash station, you would meet one weekend a month, all day Saturday and Sunday once a month. So, all those things ... And then you would become eligible for promotion after you served a certain amount of time in grade. And to be eligible for promotion, what that meant was you would ... you would come in what they call a zone ... a promotion zone. If you had been a ... been a lieutenant---senior grade for six years or three years, you were then eligible to become a lieutenant commander. And they would have what they call a selection board. And the selection board would examine every record of lieutenants. In addition to the records of lieutenants that were in the zone a year before that, that had not been promoted, they were examined again with the new group. In other words, the Navy had a theory of a funnel. You know what a funnel is shaped like? You put all the ensigns in the top of the funnel and out comes an admiral. Along the way, you have to make room. So, if you get passed over for promotion a certain amount of times, you're required to resign your commission. It's 00 ...

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: You have several awards and medals. Could you tell me about them?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Yes ... uhh ... Some of them are awards for being in the naval service. For example, there's a naval reserve medal that requires ten-year service. There is a ... There are medals given for duty in the Atlantic and, then, the Pacific during time of war. There is, also, a medal-it's an armed forces reserve medal if you were in the armed forces for a certain period of time. And there are also, the final medal, would be a World War II victory medal which was given to people at the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Do you still have those (pictures) in your possession?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Photographs? Yes, there aren't too many, because when you're in the service, especially during wartime, number-one, you're really. .. And this is going back when the cameras during that time were not really that user-friendly, number-one. Number-two, you didn't really have time. I mean you weren't ... you weren't on tour for ... as a tourist to go sight-seeing and you weren't really taking many pictures that ... that you could use later on in life.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Do your pictures still bring back memories about the war?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Yes, I think they do. Actually, I think the memories were good, because ... this probably accounted for the reason why I stayed active for so many years when I was released from active duty.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What is your fondest memory of your time as a World War II sailor in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I'm not sure. One thing that's always stayed in my mind was ... This was before the Punchbowl. .. Hawaiian There is a Hawaiian .. .it's a location---it's inside one of the craters where they have the all the war dead buried that were out there in Pearl Harbor. And I was on the top of what they call the Pali Pass, which is a high spot on this island of Oahu. And you can look down and you see these ... just fields of white crosses and it's always .. .I can still think, you know, about that.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What is your worst memory of your time serving in this war?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: The worst memory (chuckling) is...is a high line transfer. It might be humorous, because on one of my active duty tours, I ended up on an aircraft carrier---the U.S.S. Essex. It's a CVS-9. These ships were operational. In other words, if you reported for duty and they were in dry dock-well, that's where you stayed. If they were out in the ocean, or on the way out, you went with them. Now, this particular ship ... and I can't remember ...I never did find out why, but there's something in the navy called "underway replenishment", where, naturally, ships need to be replenished-they need fuel, they need stores. And how they do that is that they have ... usually, let's say if it's an oiler, designated A.D. for oiler. That ship will be on the starboard side of an aircraft carrier. And from there, they would send over whatever stores that had to be sent to that ship to replenish it. And on the other side of the oiler, on the starboard side, the right side of the oiler would usually be a destroyer getting supplies from the other side of the oiler. And naturally, behind the ships, they would all be lined up. It was when the destroyer got finished, he would just turn away from the oiler usually to starboard and the next destroyer would come up. Well, that's all very well and good when you're sending over cargo, but when you're sending over personnel, in a bosuns chair -- that's nothing but a little straight-back chair -- and you're about ...I would think its maybe thirty yards ... You can't get too close, because if you do, you're going to get a whipping motion into the water and you must have your best helmsman on duty, because you have to be on a precise course and a precise speed. And this is not done by machine. This is done by sailors on deck, pulling these ropes with these pulleys attached. It can't be a machine, because a machine can break and snap this thing. And you end up in the Atlantic. So, that's one of the scarier moments. (chuckles)

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: With all that you know now about your experiences in the Navy, would you enlist again? Why or why not?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I think so, because as I say, it was a good experience. I learned discipline. I learned how to think. I learned quite a bit and I appreciate what they were ... what I was taught. As I say, I was never ... ended. My enlistment never ended, because as a commissioned officer, I was just released to inactive duty at which point I became -- and I know it sound strange -- I became active in the inactive reserve. Much as today, you find people that are in the reserve and being ... They get called back up to different tours.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Why did your active duty end in May 1945?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I think like everything else, when the war ends ... As I say, once you became a commissioned officer, your commission would be yours until you either resigned your commission or until the navy released you completely from whatever commitment you might have had. So, as I say, I was never decommissioned or my enlistment never ended. I was just released to inactive duty. So, that's how I stayed in for another twenty some odd years, I guess.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: In retrospect, what place in history does World War II hold in your opinion?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I'm not sure. From what I see going on today, it almost seems like ... and this is my only my opinion .. .it just .. .it seems like we never learn anything. The only ... and I don't want to take a shot at whoever is running the country, but it just seems years ago, when there was a war, you depended upon your admirals and your generals, who've had nothing but experience and schooling and training for years. You depend upon them to win the war for you. Not like today when it just seems like everyone ... everyone ... all the civilians seem to have all this amazing experience in battle and where the country is being run by polls ... by ... umm".the media ... by unhappy people ... by the press. It just seems like we're not giving the people that are supposed to have the ability to win a war. We're not .. .!'m not saying that there's not ... that we haven't had problems. But, what problems do we not have in regular business today? We have people that are goofing--not doing their jobs, the same way we have in the service. But, it just seems like it's all being micro-managed or politicized, maybe is a better word. And I don't think .. .I don't think you can win a war like that.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Are you in touch with any soldiers with whom you served in the war?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Not really, because unlike a platoon with soldiers, you really move around too much, in a smaller group, usually one-on-one where you don't ... And your duty station will change. You're never in the same unit or you'll go to a different ship. So, it's a ... I think you don't get the chance to develop a friendship that you would normally ... that you would think you would develop.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What is it like to be a World War II veteran living in the United States today?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I don't know if you're familiar with my favorite poem called 'Tommy' by Rudyard Kipling (chuckling)?

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: I do know who that is, actually.

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Rudyard Kipling in eighteen whatever it was, he wrote this poem called 'Tommy'. The full name is 'Tommy Atkins'. It's supposedly a British soldier and naturally it's done in cockney accent, which I wouldn't attempt to do. But basically, what he's saying is, "Oh, it's Tommy this and Tommy that and Tommy go away, but it's thank you Mr. Atkins when the band begins to play." Now, what he's saying is, during peacetime people don't want to see you, they don't want to know you. Just get out of the way. But when the band begins to play, when war breaks out, it's thank you Mr. Atkins, and he goes on and on. I won't give you the whole poem. Uh, "It's Tommy this and Tommy that and Tommy how's your soul, but it's 'thin red line of heroes' when the drums begin to roll." In other words, when the drums begin to roll, and you're marching off to war, Then you're the 'thin red line of heroes' . But, um, in another line, he (Kipling), says, "It's Tommy this and Tommy that, and chuck him out the brute!" Get rid of him! But, it's 'savior of the country' when the guns begin to shoot." Now, this was written, what was it - 1800? - Maybe 200 years ago, and you look around today at what goes on in the government with soldiers and how they're treated, and OO .. .I have a statistic here you might be interested in, that in 1991, there were 68 men in the Senate and 48 in the House that had served in uniform at some point in this country. Fifteen years later, in 2007, there's only 29 in the Senate and 23 in the House - a drop of fifty percent, not including the nineteen or twenty thousand Congressional staffers. In other words, these people that get together and make our decisions. Now, their biggest problem today is something called entitlements. Uh, I'm sort of very funny about the word "entitlement". Now, when I receive a pension from the government for service, I don't consider that an entitlement in the sense that they consider, 00, entitlements given to, 00, uh, farmers for not growing certain crops, 00, for illegal aliens - a mother of an illegal alien. They're given social welfare support for the child who was fortunate enough to have been born at a stateside hospital, okay, so these .. .I don't consider that my service is an entitlement in the same way that what these people are getting as an entitlement. And, 00, slashing ... Slashing entitlements merely is a way to generate funds for subsidies and social spending and is not acceptable as far as I am concerned. But, I think the latest statistic I heard was that World War II veterans are dying at the rate of a thousand a day (chuckles), so it won't be long before, you know, we'll all be making everybody in Congress happy. Frankly, what I would love to see, I mean, I'm just appalled by what's going on today with, 00, the funding business. I'm just very amused. I think what would help would be to have the Senate and the Congress maybe have a meeting at Walter Reed Hospital or a naval hospital in Bethesda and let them see what I see when I go over there. These men that are being wheeled around, some with no arms and legs, some with one arm and one leg .. .I think they might change their mind a little bit. It's a pretty sad sight.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Specifically, what is the respect and acknowledgement like and what are the benefits from the government?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, as I just said, it's .... Part of my training and duty, one of the tours I took, I was a - I worked in a recruiting station, interviewing men that were looking to become commissioned or they wanted to go to officer candidate school. And they were promised certain things that are not, are not being given today. Initially, when people enlisted in World War II - and at the time you were 17 or 18 years old - you weren't thinking about retirement. You didn't envision a career of 20 years of service. You were told you would be getting certain benefits, including medical care without any cost to you for the rest of your life. Now, all ofa sudden in 1970, I don't know, 1972 or1973, Congress decided, now wait a minute. We didn't really mean that you'd get that. We meant you'd get that if it was available. Which was not what the recruiters were told, and the government sort of, I don't know, they said, "Well, the recruiters were not entitled to say what they said, because Congress is the only one that can give a benefit like that." Which was a pretty .... Which was almost like saying, "Yes, recruiters lie to you, but that's, that's the way, that's the way it's going to be."

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: How do you think the concept of war has changed between when you served in World War II and today's war in Iraq?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I think we discussed that briefly before when I said it just seems to be ... Everything is micro-managed. You sort of tie the, the military. You tie them - their hands - down, because they can't do anything without it being on the nightly news. And sure, there are, there are errors made. I understand that. But, you know, nobody is perfect. And war is a dirty, nasty, dirty, dirty thing. I mean, a war is ... You're told to go out and kill somebody. That's how you survive. Like, I see all the breast beating like Hiroshima where they have all these little ceremonies where they ring the little bells and people are ... And I'm sorry for the people that, that stood that blast over there. But, I don't see very many ceremonies commemorating the dead sailors that are still buried in the waters in Hawaii, because, they're still on the ships. They haven't gotten them out. So, ...

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What advice would you share with soldiers serving in Iraq?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I don't know. I think maybe, to sort of encourage them. That they shouldn't pay much attention to ... You see, it's so easy to say, the country this, the country that. It's not the COUNTRY, it's the government that does these things. The bulk of the American people, I'm sure, well, they're tired of the war. I don't blame them, but I think we lost, we lost more men in one day in Guadalcanal than we did in the whole war of Iraq. I mean ... So, it's ... You know, when we wentto war, we were there for 3 and 4 years, away from home. Nobody seemed to get upset about that (chuckling). But, now it's ... I don't know.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What does Memorial Day mean to you and how do you spend it?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, quietly. I, I don't do any marching any more (chuckles). Memorial Day was originally called 'Decoration Day' way back when, when ... It started when the, mostly the southerners, would decorate the graves of the Civil War dead and then it became Memorial Day when everybody was included and not just the ... (Civil War dead). And Veterans' Day, also. That's a new concept. But, it's nice to know that I can give this information to you. I mean maybe, hopefully, somebody listening will get an idea of what, what's going on and maybe, you know, try to do something about it. I don't know. We'll see.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What are your feelings about having your personal World War II experiences recorded and submitted to the Library of Congress?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: I don't have a problem with that. Ifit, if it tells people or lets them know what it was like to serve years ago and .. . You talk about gas rationing and meat rationing and all kinds of rationing and air raid drills. This country hasn't, hasn't really been tested. And maybe somebody who listens in will get a new appreciation of it, that has had somebody, an older person, that went through World War ll. Maybe they'll learn something from it. Life is a learning experience. So, who knows?

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: What other ways can our country acknowledge veterans and their sacrifices and war history besides the Veterans History Project?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Well, I, I know I sound... I don't mean to sound bitter. I was just... When I mentioned the different things that are going on ... But, it just seems like the country should take into consideration the past promises that were given and the years of sacrifice that were already made by those who've earned, earned their benefits today.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Is there anything else that you would like to share?

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Galano for participating in this Veterans' History Project.

sp.speaker: Anthony Francis Galano
sp.p: Thank you. I appreciate being able to tell my story.

sp.speaker: Christopher D. Shaheen
sp.p: Thank you very much.
